reviews: Sea Glass scoops out of a converted lifeguard hut, and the jar of sea glass by the till gets fuller every summer, because kids can trade a piece for a free taste. Take your cup to the terrace along the harbour wall and watch the ferries turn while you eat. I had blood orange and white peach. Both taste like the fruit was squeezed straight into the cup and barely sweetened, and instead of a wafer you get a handful of fresh berries on the side. Two scoops down, I was ready for the long walk out to the lighthouse.

The board is split into fruit sorbets and what they call 'creamies', and the creamies are the clever part. The salted caramel is churned on oat milk, the coconut on coconut cream, and the soft-serve machine runs on a mix of the two. Peek behind the counter and you'll see crates of oat milk and coconut cream stacked where most parlours keep the milk churns. A gull has learned to wait on the railing for dropped cones.

My son's allergist hands out a printed list of harbour spots that never handle peanuts, and Sea Glass is the only ice cream counter on it. That includes the topping jars: the crunch comes from toasted coconut, sesame brittle and sunflower seeds, and the cones are baked in the back. He has eaten his way along the whole topping row this summer.

Paper lanterns are strung along the whole pier, and the shop sits at the very end, with benches facing out to sea and a fisherman who has dangled the same line off the rail all summer without catching anything. It's mostly fruit here: a mango sorbet that's basically frozen mango, white peach, raspberry. Clean and not sticky, and every order comes with a little cup of cut melon.

The owner grew up above her parents' tofu shop, so the creamy flavours are made on soy milk from their press and there's no cow's milk in the place. The one the regulars queue for is the peanut-butter swirl: peanuts roasted in the back, ground into a ribbon and folded through the soy base in the same machine as everything else, just as the last batch of the day. You can also ask for crushed roasted peanuts from the topping tray over any scoop. The lanterns come on at dusk and the whole pier glows orange.

Wide stone steps run from the shop door down to the water, and everyone eats sitting on them with their feet just above the tideline, under striped umbrellas the staff carry out at noon. It isn't cheap: a three-scoop tasting flight costs about what a whole pizza does elsewhere on the front. The flight changes daily. Mine was blood orange, raspberry and lemon, each sharp and clean, served in tiny glass dishes with no sauce or sprinkles on top. It ate more like a bowl of fruit than a dessert.

I booked my daughter's sailing-club party here, and two of her crewmates have peanut allergies. When I ticked the allergy box on the booking form, the reply said there was nothing to change: no peanut in any base, topping or cone, and none ever goes through their machines. The crunch on top is caramelised sesame. Even the salted caramel is made with coconut cream instead of butter, and you won't find a carton of milk behind the counter. Ten kids, and one very patient pelican on the railing.

Sandpiper is a striped beach hut with a dozen deckchairs set out on the sand in front, and a boy of about ten rakes the sand smooth between customers like it's a temple garden. The board is short and fruity: lemon, raspberry, watermelon, all served in cups barely bigger than an espresso. They're bright, mostly fruit, and only just sweet, the perfect thing after a day in the sun. The board calls them sorbets, but the card taped under the till gives the real recipe: fruit, sugar and whole milk, the way the owner's grandmother made them. That's where the silkiness comes from. Strictly speaking, they're sherbets.

There's a basket by the door for any bags from the peanut cart on the boardwalk. The hut is peanut-free, toppings included, and the staff are strict about it. My sister learned the sherbet lesson the hard way. She can't do milk, assumed anything called sorbet would be fine, and spent the evening in the car with the seat tilted back.

Kittiwake is a granita counter inside the old harbour ticket office, and the original timetable boards are still up on the walls. You get five stools along an inside window ledge and nothing else. The door opens straight onto the ferry car park, so once you step out there's nowhere to sit. The granitas are lemon, watermelon and strawberry, shaved to order and barely sweet, closer to crushed fruit than dessert. Where a Sicilian bar would add a cap of whipped cream, they spoon on whipped coconut, and nothing on the board contains milk.

Years ago a regular's toddler turned out to be allergic to peanuts, and the owner took the peanut brittle off the menu that same afternoon. Peanuts never came back. The brittle now is sesame, and the open shelf behind the counter holds sugar, lemons and coconut, nothing else. My training partner carries an allergy pen and orders here without a second glance.

Low Tide parks its trailer on the old slipway, and you eat at picnic tables on the concrete while the water creeps up toward your shoes; the local game is seeing who moves first. The house special is the doughnut sundae. A sugared doughnut is fried to order, split, stuffed with three scoops of coconut soft serve, then drowned in hot fudge and topped with crumbled brownie. Even the mango and strawberry come piled on a waffle and soaked in syrup. Glorious, and afterwards I had to lie flat on the sea wall for twenty minutes.

The fudge is cocoa and coconut cream, the soft serve is coconut, and the doughnut dough is mixed with water and fried in sunflower oil, so there's no milk or butter anywhere in the trailer. I asked about peanuts for my husband, and the owner laughed: "Not in the fryer, not in the fudge, not on the counter. Never have been." He had two sundaes.

A trattoria in an old rope-maker's yard, with tables under a vine pergola and the harbour just past the gate. The chef cooks the way his Ligurian grandmother did on fast days: olive oil, never butter, cheese or cream. Trofie with basil, lemon and garlic, grilled peppers, a crisp chickpea farinata, white beans with rosemary. Everything is bright and light. My brother doesn't eat meat and had three courses to choose from.

My girlfriend gives her peanut allergy card to every waiter. Here it came back from the kitchen with a note: no peanuts or peanut oil on the premises, and all the frying is done in olive oil. The only desserts are a lemon sorbetto served in a hollowed-out lemon and a bowl of cherries. A cat lives on the rope coils by the gate and will take a breadstick if you offer one.
